input.question: Why are most orchestral pieces string dominated? And why are so many pieces written for that style of orchestra?
input.ground_truth: When brass instruments first came out they didn't have valves, so they could only hit a small variety of notes. This meant that all the melodies had to be carried by the strings, which were capable of hitting many more notes, and some like the Violin could even hit several octaves. There are some more recent pieces where the brass instruments are the ones carrying the melody, but I don't remember them off the top of my head.

Okay, let's imagine the orchestra is like a big team of friends who all play different kinds of musical instruments.

Most orchestral music has lots of string instruments—like violins, violas, cellos, and double basses—because these instruments can play very softly or very loudly, and they can play lots of different kinds of music. They can sound happy, sad, fast, or slow.

A long time ago, people liked the way these string instruments sounded together, and they wrote most of the music for them. Over time, people got used to hearing these instruments, and composers kept writing music for them because they are very flexible and can make beautiful sounds.

So, most orchestras have lots of string players, and most orchestral music is written for them because they can do so many cool things!
